snippet.title: HAM radio link budget
snippet.description:
A ham radio link budget estimates how much signal power reaches the receiver after gains and losses along the path. Start with transmitter power, add TX and RX antenna gains, then subtract cable losses and free-space path loss. For example, 100 W equals 50 dBm. With +3 dBi gain at each antenna, 1 dB TX cable loss, 120 dB path loss and 0 dB RX cable loss, the received power is about −65 dBm. Free-space path loss increases with both frequency and distance, so higher frequencies suffer more loss over the same distance. Real HF links may differ because ionospheric propagation is not pure free space.

snippet.title: This Tiny Radio Makes Backpacking Even More Fun
snippet.description:
With everything in this 14-ounce bag, I can send a radio signal thousands of miles from the backcountry. No cell service or internet connection required.

In this video, I unpack my complete HF backpacking ham radio kit, built around the tiny 5-watt QRP Labs QCX-mini. I cover the wire antenna, matching unit, battery, Morse code paddle, and everything else I bring along. Then I head outside, hang the antenna in a tree, and put it to the test.

In this video I demonstrate using roughly 30 feet of wire, my signal was picked up by automated receiving stations nearly 1,000 miles away, and eventually as far away as California, Arizona, and Florida. I use the Reverse Beacon Network website to check those reports; the radio itself doesn’t need internet to transmit. It still feels like magic to me.

I’m definitely not a Morse code expert, but experimenting with radio from camp has become one of my favorite parts of backpacking. If Morse code isn’t your thing, I’ve also linked the QRP Labs QMX below, a different model that supports voice.

snippet.title: POTA, SOTA, 911 & a Helicopter at Diamond Head | Ham Radio
snippet.description:
What started as a morning ham radio activation at Diamond Head quickly turned into a 911 call, an emergency response, and a helicopter arriving at the summit.

I want to start by recognizing the professionalism of the 911 dispatchers and Honolulu Fire Department personnel involved in this incident. From the initial 911 call through multiple follow-up calls, the dispatchers were calm, clear, and focused on getting accurate information to the responding crews. When Honolulu firefighters reached the summit, they immediately took control of the situation, assessed the patient, coordinated additional resources, and worked through the difficult logistics of getting someone safely out of the Diamond Head bunker.

Their response was impressive to watch firsthand.

My original plan that morning was much simpler.

At about 7:15 a.m., I started hiking the Diamond Head Summit Trail on Oahu to complete both a Parks on the Air (POTA) and Summits on the Air (SOTA) amateur radio activation.

I was activating:

POTA:
US-6425 — Diamond Head State Preserve
US-10913 — Diamond Head Summit State Trail

SOTA:
KH6/OH-025 — Diamond Head

Everything I needed fit into a small backpack: a 20-watt FX-4CR HF radio, Bioenno battery, end-fed wire antenna, lightweight mast, and an AnyTone VHF/UHF handheld.

After completing my 11th contact, a man approached me and asked if I was a first responder. A woman visiting from Japan had collapsed inside the bunker below the summit.

I grabbed my handheld radio, called 911, and headed down to help.

Because I wasn't sure whether I would maintain reliable cell service inside the bunker, I also advised amateur radio operators I had been communicating with to stand by in case an additional communications path was needed.

The woman's husband and adult daughter were with her. I gathered basic information and relayed it to 911 while we waited for emergency personnel to make the climb.

We were also incredibly fortunate that a paramedic and firefighter visiting from Ontario, Canada, happened to be nearby and stepped in to assist.

When the Honolulu Fire Department arrived, the firefighters quickly took over. More personnel and equipment followed, and eventually a helicopter arrived as part of the response.

Watching those crews work in the steep terrain and confined spaces of Diamond Head gave me an even greater appreciation for what our emergency responders do.

Later, I walked down the trail with the woman's daughter and helped her reconnect with her family and the emergency personnel below.

That afternoon, I received a message from the family letting me know that her mom was doing okay.

Did amateur radio make a difference that morning? Maybe. So did CERT training, Red Cross training, Scouts, emergency communications experience, and lessons learned over many years.

But probably the biggest lesson was simply this:

Be prepared, communicate clearly, and be willing to help when someone needs it.

I went up Diamond Head looking for radio contacts.

The most important contact I made that morning wasn't on the radio.

Aloha and 73,
Michael Miller, KH6ML

snippet.title: 9/11: He Stayed With the Transmitter. She Was 10 and Just Got Licensed.
snippet.description:
Free Video Course - The Top 5 Beginner Ham Radio Frustrations (and How To Overcome Them): https://hamradiolaunchpad.com/free

A ten-year-old girl got her ham radio license four days after 9/11. A broadcast engineer never made it out of the room he refused to leave. Two ham radio operators, the same week — two very different endings.

Steve Jacobson, N2SJ, kept Channel 11 on the air from the 110th floor of the World Trade Center's north tower for over twenty years — through the 1993 bombing, through equipment failures he fixed with his own shoelaces, right up until September 11th, 2001.

Four days later, ten-year-old Beverly Holtz, KC2IKT, got her license in the mail and ran a Red Cross shelter's entire radio link by herself — the very first time she'd ever been on the air.

This is both of their stories.

If you want more of these, subscribe. And if you were licensed back then, or know someone who served with their radio that week, put it in the comments — some of the best stories from that week never made it into any magazine.

The General Building (B) Examination is divided
into five major sections:

1. Planning and Estimating (15%)

• Scope of work and code compliance
• Design and construction error
identification
• Shop drawings, plans, and specifications
• Field inspection performance
• Coordination of project
• Cost estimation for materials, equipment,
and labor

2. Framing and Structural Components (20%)
• Subfloor and wall framing
• Roof framing
• Seismic hardware requirements and
installation
• Siding and stucco
• Decks and stairs

3. Core Trades (30%)
• Plumbing
• Electrical
• HVAC
• Concrete
• Earthwork and surveying
• Insulation, acoustical, and
weatherproofing
• Roofing


4. Finish Trades (20%)

• Painting, staining, coating, and interior
wall covering
• Tile and stone
• Floor covering
• Cabinetry and millwork
• Plaster, drywall, and ceilings
• Windows, skylights, and doors
• Landscaping

5. Safety (15%)
• Personnel safety
• Transportation and traffic control
• Environmental safety

snippet.title: CONFEDERATE LICENSE PLATES?!
snippet.description:
Back in April, Virginia officially ended a piece of its Confederate memorial past. Governor Abigail Spanberger signed a bill ending the state's authorization to issue or renew two specialty license plates: one honoring Confederate General Robert E. Lee as "The Virginia Gentleman," and another representing the Sons of Confederate Veterans.

The Lee plate had been on the books since 2007, passed back then with almost no opposition at all. Almost two decades later, attitudes have clearly shifted. Delegate Dan Helmer, who authored the bill, didn't soften his language when it passed, saying the Confederacy was a four year attempt by traitors to preserve slavery, and that its leaders don't deserve commemoration, let alone taxpayer support.

Current holders of either plate can keep using them until they expire, they just can't be renewed or reissued after that. Around 2,300 Virginians currently hold one of these plates.

Most Republicans opposed the bill, but a handful of House Republicans crossed over to support it. Either way, it's another sign of how much has changed in Virginia's relationship with its Confederate history over the last two decades. #virginia #racism #liberal #progressive #politicalnews #confederacy #breakingnews #trump #donaldtrump #politics

Why Ham Radio Programming Is So Frustrating (And How to Fix It)

Unboxing your first amateur handheld transceiver (HT) should feel like a high-end consumer experience, but instead, you're left staring at an LCD screen that looks like a 1990s microwave keypad[cite: 9]! Why is amateur radio programming so complicated compared to a standard GMRS or blister-pack walkie-talkie[cite: 9]? 

In this deep dive, we break down the root causes of beginner radio frustration and provide actionable solutions to get you confidently on the air. Whether you are fighting with cryptic menu structures, wrestling with counterfeit programming cables, or trying to understand the mysteries of VFO manual field programming in the field, we’ve got you covered.

**In this video, we cover:**
* **The Blank Slate Reality:** Why amateur VHF/UHF bands require total operational responsibility compared to closed, plug-and-play consumer tiers[cite: 9].
* **Decoding the Menu Maze:** Navigating flat lists, alphabetical sets, and frustrating T9-style text entry on Baofeng, Yasu, and Kenwood radios[cite: 9].
* **The Counterfeit Cable Trap:** Why Windows throws code 10 errors and how verifying an authentic **FTDI chip** saves your sanity[cite: 9].
* **USB-C Pitfalls:** The hidden difference between charge-only ports and true data ports on modern radios like the Tidradio TD-H3[cite: 9].
* **Proprietary CPS vs. Chirp:** How to leverage the open-source community spreadsheet tool safely without bricking your hardware (always download from the radio first!)[cite: 9].
* **Mastering Field Programming:** Step-by-step guidance on setting your frequency, offsets, shift directions, and cracking the CTCSS tone maze without a computer[cite: 9].
* **The Physics of Line-of-Sight:** Setting realistic range expectations for 5-watt HTs, avoiding the "silent radio error," and understanding the dangers of the reverse mode[cite: 9].
* **The Digital Future:** A quick look at how DMR, C4FM, and talk groups are expanding the hobby worldwide[cite: 9].

snippet.title: Project Mercury:  VARA alternative for high speed HF data communications
snippet.description:
Mercury is a Digital Radio OFDM protocol for HF broadcast and peer-to-peer ARQ connections with compatible TCP interfaces.  It's claim to fame is that the project is open sourced, available for multiple computer platforms, and free in all common definitions of that term.  It emulates the same software API as the popular VARA modem product, allowing it to be used in many existing systems for testing.  

Craig gives us a background in the OFDM modulation system, discusses how Mercury addresses some of the issues with the VARA product, and finishes with a live demo by sending an email with PAT Winlink hosted on a Raspberry Pi computer.

As Craig notes, this is experimental software and not yet an officially supported transport according to the developers at winlink.org.  Please reach out to the Winlink support/volunteers at winlink.org if you're interested in incorporating Mercury or other open-source/open-standard transports to help advance the art of amateur radio.   Any Mercury-related technical questions should addressed to the Rhizomatica developers at https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury and not the Winlink development team.

Craig describes himself as an "OpenSource software guy with a Linux background trying hard to blend in the radio hobby."  He is the creator of the DigiPi project, providing a variety of digital communication services over HF and VHF/UHF radios.  His work is available at https://digipi.org/ and described on his YouTube channel at  https://www.youtube.com/@UC0xIV_cFUMBxjaoBWwGNzAQ

It emulates the same software API as the popular VARA modem product, allowing it to be used in many existing systems for testing.  

Craig gives us a background in the OFDM modulation system, discusses how Mercury addresses some of the issues with the VARA product, and finishes with a live demo by sending an email with PAT Winlink hosted on a Raspberry Pi computer.

As Craig notes, this is experimental software and not yet an officially supported transport according to the developers at winlink.org.  Please reach out to the Winlink support/volunteers at winlink.org if you're interested in incorporating Mercury or other open-source/open-standard transports to help advance the art of amateur radio.   Any Mercury-related technical questions should addressed to the Rhizomatica developers at https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury and not the Winlink development team.

Craig describes himself as an "OpenSource software guy with a Linux background trying hard to blend in the radio hobby."  He is the creator of the DigiPi project, providing a variety of digital communication services over HF and VHF/UHF radios.  His work is available at https://digipi.org/ and described on his YouTube channel at  https://www.youtube.com/@UC0xIV_cFUMBxjaoBWwGNzAQ

La Oficina de Control de Activos Extranjeros, Ofac, emitió la Licencia General 5Z, la cual prorroga hasta el 5 de noviembre de 2026 la protección legal sobre las acciones de Citgo Petroleum Corp. El propósito central de esta medida es impedir que los acreedores tomen el control de la compañía.

Este instrumento jurídico sustituye a la anterior Licencia General 5Y, publicada el pasado 3 de agosto. A través de esta prórroga, se mantiene suspendida la ejecución de las garantías vinculadas al bono Pdvsa 2020, cuyo rendimiento del 8,5 % está respaldado específicamente por el 50,1 % de las acciones de la filial de Petróleos de Venezuela.

I spent three weeks trying to bridge Reticulum onto HF so two people could pass a real message hundreds of miles with no cell tower, no Starlink, and nobody in the middle charging a toll.
